problem: The answer says training error 'may rise slightly' after collecting 100 times more data. With a fixed-capacity degree-9 polynomial and about 800 points instead of 8, the model can no longer come close to interpolating the data, so training MSE rises a lot — from about 0.01 up to roughly the level of the validation error (the bias level), not slightly. The stated reason ('cannot fit every new point's noise as cheaply') also hides the real mechanism: capacity is now small compared with the sample size, so noise fitting is impossible and the training error moves down to meet the generalisation error.
fix: Training error rises substantially, from near zero toward the error of the best degree-9 fit on the true curve. With so many points relative to 10 parameters, the model can no longer interpolate, so the noise can no longer be fitted. Validation error falls because variance drops with more data. The gap between the two errors shrinks, so the overfitting largely disappears; what remains is mainly the bias of the degree-9 model.

problem: Degree 1 and degree 3 have the same gap (0.3), so a student can read this as 'gap size is the diagnostic'. The gap alone would wrongly rank the underfitting degree-1 model as equally healthy as degree 3; you also need the levels of both errors.
fix: After step 2, add one line: the degree-1 gap is also 0.3, but both its errors are high (4.2 and 4.5), so the small gap means underfitting, not a good fit. A small gap shows a healthy model only when the errors themselves are small. This is why step 4 compares the validation MSE levels.
